claims.text: For a finite simple undirected graph G with vertices n_1, ..., n_N, the adjacency matrix A has A_ij = 1 if n_i and n_j are adjacent and 0 otherwise; it is a symmetric 0-1 matrix with zero diagonal. The textbook gives the definition and the two properties; the board gives the same definition in its own letters (board V = textbook E). The board's example matrix has these properties.

claims.text: In a simple graph the i-th row sum of A equals the degree d(n_i), because the neighbours of n_i correspond one to one to the edges at n_i (no loops, no multiple edges); the diagonal entry (A^2)_{ii} equals d(n_i) because (A^2)_{ii} = sum over t of A_it A_ti = sum over t of A_it. On the board matrix the degrees are 1, 2, 1.

claims.text: Walk-counting theorem: for a simple undirected graph and every integer k >= 0, (A^k)_{ij} equals the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j (A^0 = I, the identity matrix). Proof by induction on k: the base case k = 0, and the step splits a walk of length k+1 at its last vertex before the end. Because the graph is simple, a walk is determined by its vertex sequence. The textbook has no such theorem (see C9); the proof is the paper's own, and Grinberg Theorem 4.5.10 states the multidigraph version.

claims.text: The powers of A are symmetric, (A^k)_{ij} = (A^k)_{ji}, because (A^k)^T = (A^T)^k = A^k; reading it by the theorem, reversing a walk gives a walk of the same length in the opposite direction.

claims.text: Walks are not paths. On the board graph (edges n_1n_2 and n_2n_3), (A^2)_{11} = 1 counts the walk n_1, n_2, n_1, which repeats n_1 and is therefore not a path under the course convention (Definition 1.2.13); no path of length 2 from n_1 to n_1 exists. Also (A^3)_{12} = 2 counts the walks n_1,n_2,n_1,n_2 and n_1,n_2,n_3,n_2, while a three-vertex graph has no path of length 3 (a path of length k has k+1 distinct vertices). In general (A^2)_{ii} = d(n_i) > 0 whenever n_i has a neighbour.

The theorem agrees with brute-force enumeration of walks on both graphs for k = 0 to 5 and on 200 random simple graphs with up to 6 vertices for k = 0 to 4.

claims.text: In a simple graph a walk (textbook Definition 1.2.10) is determined by its sequence of vertices, since each edge e_i = u_{i-1}u_i is fixed by its two ends; hence a walk of length k is a vertex sequence u_0, ..., u_k in which consecutive vertices are adjacent, and the length counts edges with repetition. A walk of length 0 is a single vertex. Whether the textbook admits k = 0 was not checked on the page; the paper adopts length 0 as a convention (needed for A^0 = I), as Grinberg does.
